subject: biology
title: Handling data, variables and practical safety
key_idea: A fair test changes one variable, measures one and keeps the rest the same. Repeats show how reliable results are, and means and percentage change summarise them. Graphs should be drawn with the right axes. Hazards need sensible precautions.

blocks.text: A fair test changes only one thing. This section covers the three types of variable and how a control makes results meaningful.

items.meaning: A factor you keep the same, so that it cannot affect the result.
A treatment with nothing added, used to compare with the other treatments.

diagram.alt: Sort the features of a duckweed investigation into independent, dependent and control variables.
diagram.prompt: A student investigates how the pH of pondwater affects duckweed. Sort each feature.

items.text: The number of duckweed plants after 10 days
Five duckweed plants put in each beaker at the start

items: When different volumes of a solution are added, top up with clean water so the total volume stays the same.
Use the same field or the same plants for each treatment, divided into groups. Different fields may have different soil, minerals or light.
Include a treatment with nothing added, so the other treatments can be compared with no treatment.
Change one variable, measure one variable, control the rest.
Keep the total volume the same when diluting.
A control gives a comparison.

blocks.text: Exam questions ask whether data can be trusted and how to improve an investigation.

items.meaning: The same person gets similar results when they repeat the experiment.
Another person, or different equipment or a different method, gets similar results.
A result that does not fit the pattern, also called an outlier.

items: Repeat the experiment or take repeat readings, to check the results are similar and to find a mean.
Repeat an anomalous result and leave the odd one out of the mean.
To check that a best value is correct, test a greater range of values, or smaller intervals around the best value.
Use a measuring method that does not depend on judgement, such as a colorimeter, or have the same person make all the observations.
Record units in the table headings, and put results in rank order.
Repeatable: the same person repeats it. Reproducible: someone else, or a different method.
Repeat anomalous results.
Use smaller intervals around the best value to make it more accurate.

blocks.text: Calculate a mean from repeats, and use percentage change to compare values from different starting points.

blocks.label: Mean
blocks.formula: mean = total of the values ÷ number of values
where: values are the repeat readings, in the unit measured

diagram.alt: Calculate the mean mass of DNA collected from three tests.
diagram.question: Three tests collect {a} mg, {b} mg and {c} mg of DNA. Calculate the mean mass collected. Give your answer to 1 decimal place.

blocks.label: Percentage decrease
where: starting value and final value in the same unit

items.text: Migraine days per patient fall from 9.1 to 4.4. The decrease is 9.1 − 4.4 = 4.7.

items: Use a line graph (or scatter graph) when both variables are numbers, not a bar chart or histogram.
Put the independent variable, such as time, on the x axis and the dependent variable, such as pH, on the y axis.
With several sets of results, such as three temperatures, draw one line for each set.
Mean = total ÷ number of values.
Percentage decrease = decrease ÷ starting value × 100.
Line graph, with the independent variable on the x axis.

blocks.text: A conclusion must match the data. A safe practical uses a precaution that matches the hazard.

items: Compare every treatment with the others and with the control.
A lower disease rating means less disease, so a treatment with a lower rating worked better.
Say whether each factor works on its own, and whether the combination works best.

rows: Chemicals, such as ethanol or protease
Wear a face mask or goggles
To stop them being inhaled or entering the eyes
To stop the chemicals touching the skin
The solution or tube may be hot

items: Base a conclusion on the data, including the control.
State the precaution and why it is needed.
Ethanol is flammable, so keep it away from a flame.

checks.q: A student investigates how pH affects duckweed growth. Name the independent variable and the dependent variable.
checks.a: Independent: the pH of the pondwater. Dependent: the number of duckweed plants after 10 days.

checks.q: Describe how a student could find out whether their data is repeatable and reproducible.
checks.a: Repeatable: repeat the experiment or take repeat readings. Reproducible: another person does the experiment, or use different equipment or a different method. Check that the results are similar.

checks.q: A student wants to be sure that pH 6.5 is the best pH for growth. How should they extend the experiment?
checks.a: Test other pH values, with smaller intervals around pH 6.5.

exam_phrases: repeat the experiment / take repeat readings
another student / person conducts the experiment
use different equipment / use a different method
to see if the results are the same / similar
include other / greater range / smaller intervals of pH values
keep the total / overall volume the same
turn Bunsen off as ethanol is flammable

mistakes.wrong: Draw a bar chart of the results.
mistakes.right: A bar chart or histogram is not allowed here. Draw a line or scatter graph, with time on the x axis and pH on the y axis.

mistakes.wrong: To extend the experiment, just repeat the readings.
mistakes.right: "Just repeat readings" is ignored. Include a greater range or smaller intervals of values, around the best value.

mistakes.wrong: To check the data is repeatable and reproducible, compare the results.
mistakes.right: "Compare the results" is ignored. Repeat the experiment, or have another person do it, to see if the results are the same or similar.

mistakes.wrong: Wear a lab coat in case of glass breakages.
mistakes.right: Lab coats and glass breakages are ignored. Give a precaution that matches the hazard, such as goggles for chemicals entering the eyes.

worked_example.question:
Some students investigate the effect of temperature on the decomposition of milk. Bacteria in milk have enzymes that convert sugar into lactic acid.

This is the method the students use:
• Pour 20 cm³ of milk into 3 different beakers.
• Keep each beaker in a water bath at a different temperature: 15 °C, 25 °C and 35 °C.
• Measure the pH of the milk at different times over 4 days.

The table shows their results.

Temperature (°C) | pH of milk at the start | after 12 hours | after 24 hours | after 48 hours | after 72 hours
15 | 6.5 | 6.4 | 6.3 | 6.1 | 5.8
25 | 6.5 | 6.3 | 6.2 | 5.9 | 5.5
35 | 6.5 | 6.3 | 6.1 | 5.5 | 4.9

Describe how the students should display their results in a graph.
answer_points: Draw a line graph (or scatter graph).
Put time on the x axis and pH on the y axis.
Draw three lines, one for each temperature.
worked_example.tip: Any three points score. A bar chart or histogram is not allowed, and temperature must not be on either axis.
